If your Apple CarPlay connection suddenly drops while you're driving, the problem may not lie with your iPhone, your cable, or your car.

Instead, it could be caused by radio interference.

An Axios report once detailed a strange phenomenon in Boston, where drivers would lose their CarPlay or Android Auto connection when passing through specific locations. Similar 'signal dead zones' may exist in other cities, but no one has complained about them.

The CarPlay head unit cannot independently handle GPS navigation. It maintains a direct connection with your iPhone via Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, then mirrors the display; the content on the screen relies on your phone's internet and GPS satellite connection. When the wireless connection between the head unit and the phone is disrupted, navigation fails and the connection may also drop.

Mainframe's comment received the most likes

In Grapevine, Texas, I know of a specific stretch of road between an oil depot and a nursing home where all wireless CarPlay systems crash when you drive past it. I've tried several vehicles, including those with factory-installed wireless CarPlay, cars using wireless CarPlay adapters, and aftermarket audio systems—they all stall on this stretch. Some systems recover on their own after being disrupted, while others don't. Even the latest Mercedes-Benz electric vehicles have this problem.

In the past ten years, I've only encountered this situation a few times.

Experts point out that nearby radio sources, particularly signals in the 2.4GHz band, could be the source of interference. In the case of Boston, possible culprits may include point-to-point microwave links, broadcast antennas, or unlicensed transmitters.

The key takeaway: if you frequently lose your CarPlay connection in the same spot, you may be driving through an invisible zone of radio interference. This problem may not be solvable, but knowing the cause can save you a lot of time—instead of endlessly searching for the reason or scheduling unnecessary repair services.
